stage_description: The juvenile stage runs from roughly weaning (about three weeks) to five months. It is a time of rapid growth and muscle development, when a guinea pig's personality and social bonds take shape. Sexual maturity arrives early — females can be capable of breeding at around a month of age and males a little later — so mixed-sex animals not intended for breeding are separated well in advance. Youngsters are curious, energetic, and busy exploring their territory.
nutrition: Growing youngsters still do well on alfalfa hay and young-animal pellets, which are rich in the calcium and protein that developing bones need. Introduce fresh greens and vegetables gradually, in small amounts, while watching the droppings. Because vitamin C cannot be made in the body, it must be supplied daily — through stabilised pellets and vitamin-C-rich vegetables such as bell pepper; a shortfall risks scurvy. Fresh water should always be available.
activity: Juveniles have plenty of energy and need a spacious enclosure, daily floor time in a safe, fenced area, and tunnels, hides, and things to chew. Guinea pigs are herd animals and are happiest with a same-sex companion or a compatible group. Gentle, regular handling at this age accustoms the pet to being held.
veterinary_check_frequency: A routine visit to an exotics vet helps confirm the animal's sex and assess growth rate, teeth, and skin. This is a good appointment at which to discuss neutering or spaying and the choice of compatible companions. Keep weighing your pet regularly and record the figures so that any deviation is caught early.
dental_care: The incisors and cheek teeth grow continuously for life and are worn down mainly by prolonged chewing of hay. Unlimited coarse hay is the chief safeguard against malocclusion (misaligned teeth). Make sure your juvenile eats readily and without difficulty.
warning_signs: Reasons to see a vet include refusing food, weight loss, diarrhoea, a bloated belly, and signs of vitamin C deficiency — reluctance to move, stiff or swollen joints, a rough coat, or bleeding gums. Eye or nose discharge, sneezing, hair loss, and scratching also warrant attention. Young guinea pigs weaken quickly, so a visit should not be put off.
